projectOutComesReport:
Our project successfully met its objectives in advancing materials science and detector technology, delivering outcomes with significant intellectual merit and wide-ranging societal impact. This report offers a comprehensive summary of our key achievements and findings, all made possible through the support of the National Science Foundation (NSF).

At the core of our project was the development and enhancement of Germanium (Ge) detectors, which are vital for a wide array of applications, including nuclear physics, particle physics, medical imaging, and environmental monitoring. One of the major milestones was the successful implementation of a state-of-the-art magnetron sputtering system, positioning us at the forefront of fabricating high-purity Ge detectors. These detectors are crucial for experiments aimed at detecting rare events, such as neutrinoless double-beta decay, which could offer profound insights into the fundamental properties of neutrinos.

A significant breakthrough in our project was the integration of a new automated sputtering machine, which played a pivotal role in refining the process of creating electrical contacts on Ge crystals. Through meticulous experimentation and the application of this advanced technology, we verified that this sputtering machine can reliably produce highly efficient electrical contacts. This advancement not only enhances the overall performance of the detectors, making them more sensitive and accurate, but also accelerates the research process by ensuring consistent and precise results.

The impact of the automated sputtering machine extends beyond our research in physics and materials science, significantly advancing education at institutions in the Midwest, including the University of South Dakota (USD) and South Dakota State University (SDSU). By incorporating this cutting-edge equipment into our curriculum and research activities, we provided students with invaluable hands-on experience in advanced technology, greatly enhancing their learning and better preparing them for future careers in science and engineering. During the grant period, USD successfully trained over 15 students, while SDSU trained two students. Additionally, through outreach activities, more than 20 high school students and 10 K-12 teachers visited the new sputtering machine at the USD lab, further broadening its educational impact and inspiring the next generation of scientists and educators.

Beyond technical advancements, our project offered extensive training opportunities for students and early-career researchers. By engaging them in cutting-edge research and hands-on activities—such as operating the sputtering machine and processing Ge crystals and magnetic materials—we have contributed to the development of a skilled workforce capable of driving future innovations in this field.

The broader impacts of our project extend well beyond the scientific community, influencing various aspects of society and education. One of the most notable outcomes has been the enhancement of educational experiences for students at our institution. We integrated our research findings into the curriculum, particularly in courses like Semiconductor Fundamentals and Fabrication, where students were exposed to real-world applications of the theories they were learning. This hands-on approach not only deepened their understanding but also inspired many to pursue careers in science and engineering.

Our project has also strengthened institutional infrastructure. The acquisition of advanced equipment and the enhancement of laboratory facilities have significantly improved our research capabilities, benefiting not only our current project but also future research endeavors. This development has positioned our institution as a leader in materials science and detector technology, attracting further research opportunities and collaborations.

In addition to the academic and scientific impacts, our project has potential implications for public health and environmental monitoring. The improved Ge detectors developed through our work could be used in medical imaging devices, leading to better diagnostic tools and improved patient outcomes. Moreover, these detectors could be applied in environmental monitoring systems to detect and measure radiation levels, contributing to public safety and environmental protection.

abstractText:
Humans rely on properly functioning freshwater ecosystems (e.g., streams, lakes, wetlands) for food, recreation, and drinking water. A major challenge in ecology is to understand how freshwater ecosystems will change in response to environmental disruptions. However, past efforts at measuring this change across large spatial scales are complicated by at least two challenges: 1) different places have different species, which makes it hard to compare across species when it comes to ecosystem function, and 2) collecting ecological information is extremely labor intensive, which makes it difficult to study ecological communities over space and time. This project solves those problems using cutting-edge ecological approaches. First, to overcome the limitations of species turnover, this project will measure ecosystem structure and function using animal body size distributions known as size-spectra (e.g., the relative abundance of large to small organisms), which are thought to be conserved across ecosystems regardless of species composition. Size spectra are an indicator of how efficiently energy is transferred from one organism to another in a food chain. Second, this project overcomes logistical limitations by using data already collected and curated from the National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON). Using NEON data, the researchers will analyze a large collection of size-spectra in streams over a wide range of environmental conditions to determine how stream temperature and nutrients influence freshwater ecosystems. This project is in the national interest because it provides a critical test of how freshwater ecosystems might respond to future temperature scenarios at macroecological scales. The researchers will also develop software that makes analysis of body size distributions freely available to the public and easier for ecologists to study in the future.
   
Over 50 years of research reveals a common pattern across ecosystems in which abundance (N) declines with increasing body mass (M). The shape of this relationship is described by a power law, N ~ M(exp b), known as the abundance size-spectrum, and the exponent b varies in relation to changes in energy flow through the food web. The value of b is almost always negative, suggesting a remarkably consistent ecological pattern. However, climate change is expected to alter size-spectra, based in part on shifts in body size with temperature. Despite a seemingly simple relationship of body size and temperature, experimental and field studies demonstrate disparate results for size spectra-temperature relationships, finding positive, negative, and neutral shifts in size-spectra across temperature regimes. These studies largely consist of limited samples across relatively small spatial scales, making it difficult to predict how size-spectra varies with temperature at larger scales such as continents. In addition, deviations from theoretical predictions of the b-temperature relationship may be resolved by accounting for variation in resource supply, but the effect of resource supply at large scales is also unknown. This project uses statistical modeling to determine the influence of stream temperature and resource supply on stream size spectra exponents across a broad environmental gradient represented by a national monitoring network.

projectOutComesReport:
This collaborative award examined how freshwater ecosystems respond to gradients of temperature and resources at the continental scale. To do this, the work analyzed distributions of individual body sizes in streams using data collected by the National Ecological Observatory Network. The analysis takes advantage of the fact that distributions of body size often follow a power law, a well-known pattern in ecology. However, small variations in the shape of the distributions (e.g., higher or lower frequencies of large organisms) reflect potentially large underlying changes in the food web. This project found that variation in the body size distributions of freshwater streams could only be explained by the interactions of temperature and resources. Importantly, the effect of temperature on the relative frequency of large organisms (like fish) was either neutral or positive, but never negative. This finding challenges current predictions in which warmer temperatures are expected to reduce the relative frequency of large organisms in streams. Instead, this work shows that changes to the size distribution in warmer streams depend on the availability of basal resources and these streams might support higher abundances of larger organisms if higher temperatures are also associated with higher resources at the base of the food web. The findings and techniques developed in this project go beyond analysis of NEON streams and improve approaches to freshwater management in general. For example, the work in NEON streams led directly to analysis of changes to fisheries in response to invasive carp using analyses developed with this project. 
The project trained a postdoctoral researcher and five undergraduate students. It also contributed to four undergraduate honors theses, two masters theses, and eight peer-reviewed publications. A software package for data analysis was also developed and made publicly accessible. All data and code produced in this project is permanently archived and publicly accessible.

This award is supported by the Major Research Instrumentation and the Chemistry Research Instrumentation programs as well as the Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR). The University of South Dakota is acquiring a digital camera for a transmission electron microscope (TEM) to support Professor James Hoefelmeyer and colleagues Ranjit Koodali, Chaoyang Jiang, Grigoriy Sereda and Aravind Baride. In general, a TEM sends a beam of electrons through a thin layer of material. The electron beam interacts with the substance to produce a visual image, similar to a microscope. The images are recorded by a camera and they are important for research on the chemical properties of materials. The images reveal details of the structure, such as size and shape of a nanoparticle or a protein. This information helps researchers understand the material's properties and improve them. The acquisition enhances the training of undergraduates in research. This instrument is an integral part of teaching as well as research and research training of undergraduate and graduate students at this institution and nearby universities such as South Dakota State University, Nebraska Indian Community College (NICC, in South Sioux City, Macy and Santee, NE) and Red Cloud Indian School.

The award significantly increases the capabilities and gives a new life to a heavily used transmission electron microscope. The award is aimed at enhancing research and education at all levels. It especially impacts studies controlling and characterizing plasmonic nanomaterials for surface enhanced Raman scattering and anti-counterfeiting applications. The instrumentation is also used for studying photocatalytic degradation of aqueous pollutants using nanoporous carbon materials and investigating lanthanide-doped NaYF4 (sodium ytrium tetrafluoride) upconversion nanocrystals for anti-counterfeiting applications. In addition, it provides information for exploring the use of solar fuels catalysis, fuel cells, and lithium ion batteries. The instrumentation is also used to identify antimicrobial coatings prepared by functionalized multilayered microparticles of graphene.

projectOutComesReport:
The department of chemistry at the University of South Dakota (USD) used NSF project funds to purchase a new digital camera for its transmission electron microscope (TEM). The camera was installed in April 2021 and will extend the effective life of the electron microscope by several years. The TEM enables scientists to observe and image nanoscale materials. USD Chemistry is developing advanced materials for security printing, anti-counterfeiting, fuel cells, batteries, antimicrobial coatings, and cancer imaging and treatment. New nanomaterials discoveries include gold nanostars, enzyme-responsive mesoporous silica nanoparticles as targeted drug carriers, luminescent polymer and carbon nanoparticles, lanthanide doped sodium yttrium fluoride (NaYF4) nanocrystals, hollow nanoparticles of manganese oxide (Mn3O4), nanocrystal junctions of nickel oxide (NiO) or silver (Ag) with titanium oxide (TiO2), nanostructured calcium carbonate (CaCO3) and hydroxyapatite (Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2), and modified graphene. The project led to two US patent applications with a patent granted for a new method and composition to treat cancer. We are training students to enter the STEM workforce and inspiring members of the community to understand and appreciate the work of scientists, the tools scientist use, and opportunities available to become a scientist. Annual participants include undergraduate students in laboratory courses from first-year Honors General Chemistry Laboratory to upper level Inorganic Chemistry Laboratory, undergraduate students participating in research projects, including participants in the NSF:REU Site hosted by USD Chemistry, graduate students, high school teachers and students, and faculty.

abstractText:
All NSF funded grants have the potential to not only advance scientific knowledge but also contribute to the achievement of socially relevant outcomes.  Socially relevant scientific outcomes are referred to as Broader Impacts. Education, training, collaboration, broadening participation and raising awareness of the role that science plays in the quality of everyday life are broader impacts that promote science literacy in society.  The National Science Foundation places great importance on the communication of science and its potential to benefit society. While broader impacts are of great importance, achieving them at scale requires addressing challenges in planning and implementing activities that include: 1) finding and sharing resources (funding, infrastructure and personnel); 2) locating and collating information that is diverse, widespread and presented in a variety of ways; 3) addressing the lack of technical expertise and infrastructure for creating websites, videos, and integrating applications such as social media, survey tools and analytic tools; 4) disseminating information and interacting with large, distributed groups; 5) meeting recruitment initiative goals to broaden participation and building collaborations in unfamiliar communities; and 6) measuring success and promoting successful projects. The primary objective of this workshop is to address these issues by exploring the creation of an integrated Gateway for Education, Training, Broader Impacts and Outreach for EPSCoR jurisdictions that would provide infrastructure for researchers, educators, students, project managers, and the general public to access, create, and share information about broader impact activities and resources. 

Strategies for realizing the Broader Impacts (BI) of scientific research include using cyberinfrastructure to empower knowledge dissemination, activating effective jurisdictional and regional collaborations that advance scientific research, broadening participation in science, technology and engineering and mathematics (STEM), expanding the scientific literacy of all citizens, and disseminating the importance of STEM research and education. The primary objective of this workshop is to assess the state of the art in existing resources to promote BI, and explore creating an integrated Gateway for Education, Training, Broader Impacts and Outreach for EPSCoR jurisdictions that would provide infrastructure for researchers, educators, students, project managers, and the general public to access, create, and share information about broader impact activities and resources.  Participants will achieve the following during this event: 1) identify BI and outreach needs of the EPSCoR community; 2) identify, introduce, and evaluate BI resources and tools from well-established groups such as the Center for the Advancement of Informal Science Education and the Institute for Broadening Participation; 3) identify what functionality gaps exist in the current BI platforms that are required by the EPSCoR community; 4) create a set of BI “user stories” (i.e. use cases) that would be used to document the requisite functionality; 5) discuss how the development of a EPSCoR BI network could be integrated into a Hub or Ecosystem for the broader community; and  6) identify funding opportunities to develop, pilot test, scale and sustain the system.  The outcomes of this project will elevate the visibility and importance of broader impact activities, and their intertwined research activities, in a scalable and transformative way.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

The National Science Foundation funded our NSF 1903738 EPS-WO workshop proposal to allow us to explore creating an integrated Gateway for Education, Training, Broader Impacts and Outreach for EPSCoR jurisdictions. This platform would provide infrastructure for researchers, educators, students, project managers, and the public to access, create, and share information about broader impact activities and resources.

 The genesis of this idea was through the National Science Foundation Plant Genome Research Program funded project, NSF IOS-1545596 EAGER: GETBIO-PGR Gateway for Education, Training, Broader Impacts and Outreach in Plant Genome Research (https://getbiopgr.org/) developed by two of the workshop PIs. The GETBIO-PGR platform was developed to enable PGRP researchers to share the full range of their broader impact activities within a centralized, integrated infrastructure. GETBIO-PGR offers a novel resource for more efficient scaling of broader impacts collaborations allowing researchers, educators, students and the general public to access, create, share and exchange information about research projects? broader impact activities. This platform makes it possible to provide more rapid dissemination and more effective use of resources such as best practices for mentoring, workshop management, and data analysis along with an increase in peer-to-peer interactions at all levels, from undergraduate students to faculty. Additionally, GETBIO-PGR provides the ability for users with a Bioinformatics Tool Discovery System (Bio-TDS). Bio-TDS was developed to assist researchers in retrieving the most applicable analytic tools by allowing them to formulate their questions as free text. The Bio-TDS is a flexible retrieval system that affords users from multiple bioscience domains (e.g. genomic, proteomic, bio-imaging) the ability to query over 15 000 analytic tool descriptions integrated from well-established, community repositories. One of the primary components of the Bio-TDS is the ontology and natural language processing workflow for annotation, curation, query processing, and evaluation.

 The Established Program to Stimulate Competitive Research (EPSCoR) Research Infrastructure Improvement Track-1 (RII Track-1) awards support improvements to cyber infrastructure and human capital development in research areas and welcomes proposals for workshops from institutions within EPSCoR-eligible jurisdictions. Education, training, collaborations, broadening participation as well as raising awareness of the role that science plays in the quality of everyday life have remained important goals of EPSCoR. Strategies for achieving the EPSCoR objectives include the utilization of cyberinfrastructure to empower knowledge dissemination, activate effective jurisdictional and regional collaborations that advance scientific research, broaden participation in science and engineering by institutions, organizations, and people within EPSCoR jurisdictions, expand the scientific literacy of all citizens, and disseminate to them the importance of STEM research and education [1]. All NSF funded grants have the potential to not only advance scientific knowledge through research but also contribute to the achievement of societally relevant outcomes ? what NSF calls Broader Impacts.

 The results of our NSF 1903738 EPS-WO workshop have the potential to elevate the visibility and importance of broader impact activities -- and their intertwined research activities -- in a scalable, transformative way. The focus of the workshop was to: 1) identify the Broader Impact (BI) and outreach needs of the EPSCoR community; 2) identify, introduce, and evaluate BI resources and tools from well-established groups such as the Center for the Advancement of Informal Science Education and the Institute for Broadening Participation; 3) identify what functionality gaps exist in the current BI platforms that are required by the EPSCoR community; 4) create a set of BI questions that would be used to document the requisite functionality; 5) discuss how the development of a BI platform could be integrated into a Hub/Ecosystem for the broader community; and 6) identify funding opportunities for future development and sustainability.

 Through our NSF 1903738 EPS-WO funding, we convene an NSF EPSCoR workshop to explore creating an integrated Gateway for Education, Training, Broader Impacts and Outreach for EPSCoR jurisdictions that would provide infrastructure for researchers, educators, students, project managers, and the general public to access, create, and share information about broader impact activities and resources. Approximately 100 participates took part in the workshop activities. There were nineteen EPSCoR jurisdictions represented and eight outside organizations. The workshop activities resulted in the formation of three specific working groups and one overarching working group. These working groups are organized around the questions identified by the workshop participants:
